slo_title: Define the architecture and purpose of exokernel and layered operating systems

options.A: Flat organization with no separation of services
options.B: Services built on top of each other in hierarchical layers
options.C: Direct hardware access by all services
options.D: All services run at the same privilege level

mcq.answer_text: Services built on top of each other in hierarchical layers

options.A: To execute only system-level code securely
options.B: To run guest operating systems on virtualized hardware
options.C: To provide a direct interface to hardware for all applications
options.D: To prevent multiprogramming on a host system

mcq.answer_text: To run guest operating systems on virtualized hardware

options.A: Implemented inside the kernel for performance
options.B: Shifted to user-level libraries or applications

mcq.answer_text: Shifted to user-level libraries or applications

options.C: Monolithic blocks running in user mode
options.D: Kernel extensions loaded only at boot time

options.A: Lack of device drivers in the kernel
options.B: Direct hardware access given to applications increases security risks

mcq.answer_text: Direct hardware access given to applications increases security risks

answer: A Hypervisor manages Virtual Machines by allocating hardware resources, controlling execution, and isolating VMs from each other, ensuring secure and efficient virtualization.
Unlike Monolithic and Microkernels that abstract hardware resources, the Exokernel exposes hardware resources directly to applications while enforcing access control, offering minimal abstraction.

lq.q: Compare Modular Kernel and Virtual Machines based on architecture, purpose, advantages, and limitations. Explain how they differ in resource management and system isolation.
answer: Aspect
Modular Kernel
Virtual Machines (VMs)
Definition
An operating system kernel designed to load and unload kernel modules dynamically at runtime.
A software-emulated environment that allows multiple OS instances to run on the same hardware.
Primary Purpose
To enhance flexibility, maintainability, and extensibility of the operating system.
To provide system-level virtualization with isolation between guest OS instances.
Architecture
Core kernel with loadable modules (e.g., device drivers, file systems) that operate in kernel space.
Uses a Hypervisor (Type 1 or Type 2) to manage multiple virtualized OS instances on shared hardware.
Resource Management
Handled within a single OS instance through modular components; shares system resources under one kernel.
Hypervisor allocates hardware resources (CPU, memory, I/O) to each VM, allowing independent management.
System Isolation
Limited — all modules share the same kernel space; faults in modules can affect the entire system.
High — Each VM operates as a separate system with its own OS, ensuring strong fault and security isolation.
Performance
High — operates close to hardware with minimal abstraction.
May have overhead due to virtualization layer but enables multi-OS deployment.
Flexibility
Modules can be added or removed without rebooting the OS.
Can run different operating systems and isolated environments on the same hardware.
Security
Moderate — vulnerabilities in kernel modules may affect the whole system.
High — VMs are isolated; compromise in one VM does not directly affect others or the host.
Example OS/Tools
Linux with Loadable Kernel Modules (LKMs), BSD kernel modules.
VMware ESXi, KVM, VirtualBox, Hyper-V.
Limitations
Kernel crashes due to faulty modules; limited isolation.
Performance overhead, complex resource allocation, requires hypervisor management.
